summary: This bill amends the Clayton Act to allow state attorneys general to sue companies for damages on behalf of their residents injured by price discrimination violating the Robinson-Patman Act.

scores.thoughts: The bill amends the Clayton Act to allow state attorneys general to bring parens patriae civil actions for damages from Robinson-Patman Act violations (price discrimination). It involves no appropriations, budgets, or fiscal expenditures; it only expands legal authority for lawsuits. No impact on government spending levels.
The bill concerns antitrust enforcement via civil lawsuits for price discrimination, not taxes, tax rates, or revenue collection. No mention of taxation.
No provisions related to healthcare, insurance, coverage, or medical services. Purely antitrust law amendment.
No reference to firearms, regulations, or rights. Unrelated.
No immigration, borders, or pathways mentioned. Antitrust focus only.
No abortion-related content. Civil antitrust amendment.
No military, defense, or spending provisions. Domestic business competition law.
No environmental protections, regulations, or climate issues. Price discrimination enforcement.
No welfare, food stamps, or safety net programs. Legal remedy expansion for businesses/consumers.
No education funding, schools, or choice provisions. Antitrust only.
No drugs, decriminalization, or enforcement. Civil price discrimination suits.

This is a civil antitrust amendment allowing state AG parens patriae suits, not criminal penalties, sentencing, policing, or justice reform. Robinson-Patman has criminal aspects but this bill specifies civil damages actions.

Robinson-Patman Act addresses domestic price discrimination between buyers (e.g., protecting small retailers from chain store discounts), not international trade, tariffs, free trade agreements, or protectionism in imports/exports. Domestic competition policy, not trade policy.
No deficit spending, debt reduction, or fiscal policy. Only legal authority change.
No LGBTQ+ protections or limitations. Business antitrust.
No foreign aid or international assistance. U.S. domestic law.
No voting access, elections, or integrity measures. Unrelated.
No technology regulation, data privacy, or oversight. General antitrust for price discrimination.
Focuses on small business protection from price discrimination by large sellers, not workers, unions, protections, or employer flexibility. Business-to-business competition, not labor.
No religious exemptions, civil rights, or discrimination issues. Antitrust enforcement.
